cards.q: Which layer delivers data to the right program on a machine, and with what address?
cards.a: The transport layer, using port numbers.

cards.q: What does a router in the middle of the internet look at to forward a packet?
cards.a: The IP header: the destination IP address. It does not look at TCP or application data.

cards.q: With a 1500-byte MTU, how much application data fits in one TCP packet without options?
cards.a: 1460 bytes: 1500 minus 20 for IPv4 and 20 for TCP.

cards.q: Why do games care so much about header overhead?
cards.a: Their messages are small and frequent, so headers can be larger than the data itself.

cards.q: What is the network address of 10.20.30.40/20?
cards.a: 10.20.16.0: the mask 255.255.240.0 keeps 10.20 and the top 4 bits of 30 (16).

cards.q: How many usable hosts does a /26 network have?
Why can't an outside computer start a connection to a laptop behind a home router?
cards.a: NAT only has mappings for connections started from inside; an unsolicited packet has nowhere to go.

cards.q: What is the difference between a recursive resolver and an authoritative server?
cards.a: The resolver answers clients by looking things up and caching them; the authoritative server holds the actual records for a zone.

cards.q: Which record type holds an IPv6 address?
cards.a: AAAA.

cards.q: Encode the name a.bc as DNS labels.
Why should a program use getaddrinfo instead of sending its own DNS queries?
cards.a: It uses the system's resolver, cache and hosts file and handles both IPv4 and IPv6 correctly.

cards.q: What are the three packets of the TCP handshake?
cards.a: SYN, then SYN+ACK, then ACK.

cards.q: What does a TCP acknowledgement number tell the sender?
cards.a: That every byte before that number has arrived, and which byte the receiver expects next.

cards.q: What is head-of-line blocking?
cards.a: When one TCP segment is lost, all data after it waits for the retransmission, even if it already arrived.

cards.q: Why do fast-paced games send state over UDP?
cards.a: Lost updates are soon obsolete, and waiting for retransmissions would delay newer, more useful data.

cards.q: What does the default gateway do for your computer?
cards.a: It receives every packet whose destination is not on the local network.

cards.q: Routes 172.16.0.0/12 and 172.16.5.0/24 both match 172.16.5.9. Which is used?
cards.a: 172.16.5.0/24, the longer prefix.

cards.q: How does traceroute find the routers along a path?
cards.a: It sends packets with increasing TTL values; each router that drops one with TTL zero reports back.

cards.q: A protocol needs 4 round trips and the RTT is 80 ms. Roughly how long does it take, however fast the bandwidth?
cards.a: About 320 ms: latency, not bandwidth, decides it.

cards.q: Why try every address getaddrinfo returns?
cards.a: A name can have several addresses (IPv6 and IPv4, several servers); some may be unreachable from where you are.

cards.q: send returns 512 when you asked it to send 2000 bytes. What does that mean?
cards.a: Only 512 bytes were accepted; you must send the remaining 1488 yourself.

cards.q: What does recv returning 0 mean?
cards.a: The other side has closed its sending direction: the end of the stream.

cards.q: connect fails with error 10061. What is the likely cause?
cards.a: Nothing is listening on that port at that address: connection refused.

cards.q: What does accept return?
cards.a: A new socket for the accepted connection; the listening socket carries on listening.

cards.q: Why does a test that sends one small message over loopback hide framing bugs?
cards.a: Small messages usually arrive in one recv locally; over a real network they can be split or joined.

cards.q: Why call shutdown(s, SD_SEND) before closesocket?
cards.a: It tells the peer you have finished sending while still letting you receive its remaining data, avoiding a reset that could lose data.

cards.q: A restarted server fails to bind with WSAEADDRINUSE. What might be the cause?
cards.a: Connections from the previous run are still in TIME_WAIT on that port.

cards.q: How is the port 443 (0x01BB) written in network byte order?
cards.a: 01 BB: big-endian, most significant byte first.

cards.q: What does the first byte 0x46 of an IPv4 header say?
cards.a: Version 4, header length 6 words (24 bytes), so it carries 4 bytes of options.

cards.q: Name two reasons not to cast a packet buffer to a C++ struct.
cards.a: Any two of: padding, host byte order, implementation-defined bit-field order, misaligned reads and aliasing violations.

cards.q: How do you check an Internet checksum?
cards.a: Sum all 16-bit words including the checksum with one's complement addition; a correct packet gives 0xFFFF.

cards.q: What does WSAEWOULDBLOCK from recv on a non-blocking socket mean?
cards.a: No data is available right now; it is not an error.

cards.q: What does an event loop wait in, and why?
cards.a: In select or WSAPoll, which sleep until any socket is ready, so the loop uses no CPU while idle.

cards.q: Why does each connection need its own output queue in an event loop?
cards.a: send may accept only part of the data or none; the rest must wait until the socket is writable again.

cards.q: Why must an event loop never do slow work inline?
cards.a: While it works, it serves no other connection; every client waits.

cards.q: How many datagrams can one recvfrom return?
cards.a: Exactly one, whole; never part of one and never two.

cards.q: Why keep UDP payloads under about 1200 bytes?
cards.a: Larger datagrams are fragmented, and losing any fragment loses the whole datagram.

cards.q: Which two things must an answer to a UDP request match before it is accepted?
cards.a: The address and port it was sent to, and the request's id.

cards.q: What does WSAECONNRESET on a UDP socket mean on Windows?
cards.a: An earlier datagram reached a port where nothing listens and an ICMP port unreachable came back; it can be ignored.

cards.q: What ends the headers of an HTTP/1.1 message?
cards.a: An empty line: \r\n on its own.

cards.q: Why is the Host header required in HTTP/1.1?
cards.a: One server address can host many websites; Host says which one the request is for.

cards.q: A client receives status 418 and does not know it. How should it treat it?
cards.a: As a generic 4xx client error, like 400.

cards.q: Why must every response on a persistent connection have a Content-Length or chunked body?
cards.a: Otherwise the client cannot tell where the response ends and the next one begins.

cards.q: How does a parser know it has received all the headers?
cards.a: It has found the empty line: the first \r\n\r\n in the stream.

cards.q: A response has Content-Length: 120 and Transfer-Encoding: chunked. What should a strict parser do?
cards.a: Reject it as ambiguous; this combination enables request smuggling.

cards.q: Decode the chunk sizes 4, 6 and E.
cards.a: 4, 6 and 14 bytes: chunk sizes are hexadecimal.

cards.q: A GET request has no Content-Length and no Transfer-Encoding. How long is its body?
cards.a: It has no body.

cards.q: Which part of a URL is never sent to the server?
cards.a: The fragment, after #.

cards.q: How is the character é percent-encoded?
cards.a: As its UTF-8 bytes: %C3%A9.

cards.q: Why decode each part of a URL only after splitting it at its separators?
cards.a: An encoded separator such as %2F is data; decoding first would turn it into a real separator.

cards.q: In form encoding, how are a space and a plus sign written?
cards.a: A space as +, and a plus sign as %2B.

cards.q: A path matches a route but the method does not. What status should the server send?
cards.a: 405 Method Not Allowed, with an Allow header listing the allowed methods.

cards.q: Why should a server send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff?
cards.a: So browsers use the declared Content-Type instead of guessing, which could turn data into executable content.

cards.q: Why reject a .. that climbs above the root instead of clamping it?
cards.a: It is never a legitimate request; rejecting it makes the attack visible and avoids subtle mistakes in the clamping.

cards.q: Name two Windows-specific things a file server must reject in paths.
cards.a: Any two of: backslashes, colons (drive letters and alternate data streams), device names like CON or NUL, names ending in a dot or space.

cards.q: What three guarantees does TLS add to a connection?
cards.a: Confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the server.

cards.q: Does *.justloofy.dev match a.b.justloofy.dev?
cards.a: No: a wildcard matches exactly one label.

cards.q: Why does the ClientHello carry the hostname (SNI)?
cards.a: One address can host many sites, and the server must pick the right certificate before any HTTP is sent.

cards.q: Why is turning off certificate verification never an acceptable fix?
cards.a: Without it anyone can impersonate the server, so the encryption only protects your data for the attacker.

cards.q: What is the difference between a capture filter and a display filter?
cards.a: A capture filter decides what is recorded; a display filter only hides packets from view and can be changed afterwards.

cards.q: A pcap file's magic number reads as 0xD4C3B2A1. What does that mean?
cards.a: The file was written in the other byte order: every field must be read big-endian.

cards.q: Why can a packet's captured length be smaller than its original length?
cards.a: The capture stored at most the snapshot length of each packet.

cards.q: What must you enable to capture traffic to 127.0.0.1 on Windows?
cards.a: Npcap's loopback capture support (the loopback adapter).

cards.q: An Ethernet frame's bytes 12-13 are 86 DD. What comes next?
cards.a: An IPv6 header.

cards.q: The first byte of an IPv4 header is 0x47. Where does the TCP header start?
cards.a: 28 bytes into the IP header: IHL is 7 words.

cards.q: Why use the IPv4 total length instead of the frame's length to find the end of the data?
cards.a: Short frames are padded to the Ethernet minimum; the padding is not part of the IP packet.

cards.q: Which IPv4 fragments carry the TCP header?
cards.a: Only the first one, with fragment offset 0.

cards.q: A TCP flags byte is 0x12. Which flags are set?
cards.a: SYN and ACK (0x02 + 0x10).

cards.q: The data offset nibble is 8. Where does the payload start?
cards.a: 32 bytes into the TCP header: 20 bytes of fixed header and 12 bytes of options.

cards.q: Why does a SYN with no data still use a sequence number?
cards.a: SYN and FIN each count as one byte of sequence space, so they can be acknowledged.

cards.q: Why do captures on the sending machine often show bad TCP checksums?
cards.a: The network card fills in the checksum after the capture point (checksum offloading).

cards.q: How do you put both directions of one connection under the same key?
cards.a: Order the two endpoints canonically, for example the lower address and port first.

cards.q: A server's SYN-ACK has relative ack 1. What does it acknowledge?
cards.a: The client's SYN, which used sequence number 0.

cards.q: How does a retransmission appear in a capture?
cards.a: As a segment whose sequence range was already sent earlier in that direction.

cards.q: A SYN is answered immediately by a RST. What happened?
cards.a: Connection refused: nothing was listening on that port.

cards.q: In a DNS header, how do you tell a query from a response?
cards.a: By the top bit of the flags, QR: 0 for a query, 1 for a response.

cards.q: What does a TLS record with content type 23 contain?
cards.a: Encrypted application data.

cards.q: Where in a capture can you see which website an HTTPS connection was for?
cards.a: In the server name indication extension (type 0) of the ClientHello.

cards.q: Why must a decoder check every length field against the bytes available?
cards.a: Captured data can be truncated or malformed; trusting a length would read past the end.

cards.q: What is head-of-line blocking?
cards.a: When one lost TCP segment holds back all later data, even though it has arrived, until the lost one is retransmitted.

cards.q: Why is resending an old player position pointless?
cards.a: Newer positions have been sent since; only the latest state matters.

cards.q: How does a UDP "connection" end?
cards.a: By timing out after hearing nothing for a while, since there is no FIN.

cards.q: Why make the network simulator deterministic?
cards.a: So a failing test produces the same packet losses every time and can be debugged.

cards.q: Why does `a > b` fail for sequence numbers?
cards.a: After the counter wraps, a newer packet has a smaller number than an older one.

cards.q: What is `sequenceDifference(1, 65535)`?
cards.a: 2: packet 1 is two newer, across the wrap.

cards.q: A packet arrives whose number is 500 behind the latest, with a 256-number window. What happens?
cards.a: It is dropped: it is too old to tell whether it is a duplicate.

cards.q: Why might a game drop a late position update but still read the chat message in the same packet?
cards.a: Positions are newest-wins, so old ones are useless; chat messages must each be delivered.

cards.q: With ack = 200 and only bit 0 of ackBits set, which packets were received?
Why put acknowledgements in every packet instead of sending separate ack packets?
cards.a: Both sides send constantly anyway, so acks cost only a few header bytes, and the repetition protects them from loss.

cards.q: The latest is 50 and packet 90 arrives. What happens to the bits?
cards.a: The jump is 40, more than 32, so every old bit falls off the field, including the one for 50 (it would be bit 39): the bits become 0.

cards.q: Why must the sender remember which packets were already acknowledged?
cards.a: Each packet is acknowledged by many incoming packets, but should produce its delivered event only once.

cards.q: The first RTT sample is 80 ms. What are srtt, rttvar and the timeout?
cards.a: srtt 80 ms, rttvar 40 ms, timeout 80 + 160 = 240 ms (before clamping).

cards.q: Why add 4 × rttvar to the timeout rather than using srtt alone?
cards.a: So a normal but slower-than-average round trip is not treated as a loss.

cards.q: What does Karn's rule say?
cards.a: Do not take an RTT sample from anything that was retransmitted, since the ack is ambiguous.

cards.q: A receiver expecting message 10 receives 12, then 10. What is delivered and when?
cards.a: Nothing at 12 (it is buffered); at 10, message 10 is delivered, and 12 waits for 11.

cards.q: Why not let IP fragment large UDP datagrams?
cards.a: Losing any fragment loses the whole datagram, some networks drop fragments, and IPv6 routers do not fragment.

cards.q: A fragment says index 7, count 5. What should the receiver do?
cards.a: Drop it: the index must be below the count.

cards.q: Why do incomplete blocks need a timeout?
cards.a: A lost fragment, or a malicious sender, would otherwise keep reassembly buffers in memory forever.

cards.q: What does a priority accumulator guarantee that plain priorities do not?
cards.a: Low-priority objects still get sent eventually, because their score keeps growing until they are.

cards.q: Why do clients send inputs rather than positions?
cards.a: So the server computes the results itself; a client cannot simply claim where it is or what it hit.

cards.q: A client sends a movement vector of length 3. What should the server do?
cards.a: Clamp it to the allowed maximum (length 1); never trust input values as they arrive.

cards.q: Why cap the number of ticks run in one frame?
cards.a: To avoid a spiral where catching up takes so long that the next frame falls even further behind.

cards.q: What does `alpha` in the accumulator loop represent?
cards.a: How far the current time is between the last tick and the next, used to blend states for drawing.

cards.q: A map is 0 to 4 096 units wide and positions use 16 bits. What is the step size?
cards.a: About 4 096 / 65 535, roughly 0.06 units.

cards.q: Why should the server simulate with quantised values?
cards.a: So the state the client reconstructs matches the server's exactly, instead of drifting by rounding errors.

cards.q: Why encode against the last acknowledged snapshot rather than the last one sent?
cards.a: The last one sent might have been lost; the acknowledged one is known to be on the client.

cards.q: What does an entity look like in a delta if it has not changed?
cards.a: It is not included at all.

cards.q: Why render other players in the past?
cards.a: So the client already has snapshots on both sides of the render time and can blend smoothly, even with jitter and the odd lost snapshot.

cards.q: With snapshots at 20 per second, what delay is typical?
cards.a: About 100 ms, two snapshot intervals.

cards.q: Why use the server's tick numbers instead of arrival times?
cards.a: Arrival times include network jitter; the tick numbers are the times the states really belong to.

cards.q: Why limit extrapolation?
cards.a: Guesses grow wrong quickly, causing visible snapping when the real state arrives.

cards.q: What does the server need to include for reconciliation to work?
cards.a: The authoritative state of the player and the sequence number of the last input it applied.

cards.q: Why replay pending inputs instead of just jumping to the server's position?
cards.a: The server's state is a round trip old; replaying the unconfirmed inputs brings it back to the present.

cards.q: Prediction was perfect. What does reconciliation change on screen?
cards.a: Nothing: the replay arrives at the same position.

cards.q: Why should the client not predict whether its shot killed someone?
cards.a: Hits decide the game, depend on other players' true positions, and must be decided by the server.

cards.q: Why would a perfectly aimed shot miss without lag compensation?
cards.a: The shooter sees the target in the past; by the time the shot reaches the server, the target has moved.

cards.q: What does the server need to store to rewind?
cards.a: A short history of each player's position (hitbox) per tick.

cards.q: A client claims it was seeing tick 1 000 while the server is at tick 5 000 and allows 32 ticks of rewind. Which tick is used?
cards.a: 4 968, the oldest allowed.

cards.q: Who gets the advantage of lag compensation, and what does the other side experience?
cards.a: The shooter; the target can be hit after reaching cover on their own screen.
